definition: Cognitive robotics or cognitive technology is a subfield of robotics concerned with endowing a robot with intelligent behavior by providing it with a processing architecture that will allow it to learn and reason about how to behave in response to complex goals in a complex world.
details: Cognitive robotics may be considered the engineering branch of embodied cognitive science and embodied embedded cognition, consisting of robotic process automation, artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, optical character recognition, image processing, process mining, analytics, software development and system integration.

explainer.lead: Cognitive robotics aims to build robots that can learn and reason about what to do, rather than merely follow fixed instructions. The goal is intelligent behavior in response to complex goals and complicated surroundings.

tiers.eli5: Imagine asking a toy robot to tidy a messy room instead of making it follow the same path every time. It would need to notice what had changed, think about what to do next, and learn from experience. Cognitive robotics is about giving robots that kind of thinking-and-learning ability.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers apply the idea by integrating technologies such as machine learning, deep learning, image processing, optical character recognition, analytics, and process mining into a robot's processing architecture. Software development and system integration connect these capabilities to goal-directed behavior. A key pitfall is treating the presence of AI components as sufficient: the architecture must support learning and reasoning about behavior in a complex world.
tiers.paperLevel: In plain-text terms, given complex goals g and a complex world w, cognitive robotics seeks a processing architecture A that enables learning and reasoning to produce intelligent behavior b. It can be viewed as the engineering branch of embodied cognitive science and embodied embedded cognition. The definition is architectural rather than algorithmic and does not prescribe one particular learning or reasoning method.

explainer.example: Consider a robot given the goal of clearing objects from a cluttered table. Image processing helps it identify the objects, while its cognitive architecture reasons about which object to move next and uses learning to improve its behavior rather than relying only on a fixed sequence.

explainer.intuition: A conventional automated system can follow a predetermined routine, but a cognitive robot needs a way to work out how to behave. Its processing architecture connects goals and information about the world with learning, reasoning, and action.
howItWorks: Start with a complex goal and a robot situated in a complex world.
Process information about that world using capabilities such as image processing or optical character recognition.
Use the processing architecture to learn and reason about possible behavior.
Select and carry out behavior directed toward the goal.
Integrate the necessary software and AI components so they operate as one system.
explainer.whyItMatters: It addresses the gap between executing predefined instructions and behaving intelligently when goals and surroundings are complicated. It also links robotics with embodied approaches to cognition through engineering.
misconceptions: It is not simply any robot that performs a task automatically.
It is not a single machine-learning algorithm; its focus is a processing architecture.
Including AI components alone does not establish learning and reasoning about behavior.
